_comment: Sound WS1 - no printed key; answers DERIVED from physics.

_excluded_figures.desc: CRO trace waveform + four displacement-time graph options (softer/lower-freq note)
Four velocity-vs-pressure graph options for gas at constant temperature
Displacement-time graph of an instrument + four waveform graph options (same pitch, different quality)
Diagram of two sound waves Wave X and Wave Y (compare frequency/pitch)
Four y-vs-t graph options for a wave of amplitude 5 cm, frequency 100 Hz

1.reason: In a 10x10x10 m room the path difference (~20 m) gives a reflection delay of only ~0.067 s (<0.1 s), so the reflected sound merges with the original; the ear's persistence of hearing (~0.1 s) prevents a separate echo.

2.reason: Absorbent materials reduce multiple reflections so the echo/reverberation effect is minimized and speech stays clear.

3.reason: A pulse is a single short-duration disturbance created in a small part of the medium.

5.reason: Bats and dolphins produce and use ultrasonic sound (frequency > 20 kHz).

6.reason: String->Sitar(iii), Membrane->Tabla(i), Air column->Flute(iv), Plate->Bicycle bell(ii): (a)-iii,(b)-i,(c)-iv,(d)-ii = option D.

7.reason: Speed of sound rises with temperature; Chennai is hotter so v_c would be higher than v_d. Wait: hotter -> faster, so v_c > v_d. REVIEW: option C (v_c > v_d) is the temperature-correct choice for a hotter Chennai.

9.reason: Infrasound (<20 Hz) is perceived/used by large animals such as rhinoceros (also elephants, whales); humans, rats and bats cannot hear it.

10.reason: Music has a pleasant, regular waveform vs noise's irregular one; they differ in quality (timbre/regularity).

11.reason: SONAR uses ultrasonic waves (high frequency, less diffraction, directional).

12.reason: Infrasonic (<20 Hz) -> audible -> ultrasonic (>20 kHz): the terms denote increasing frequency.

13.reason: Insect sound is ultrasonic (f > 20 kHz), so lambda < 340/20000 = 1.7x10^-2 m. The only option below this (a smaller wavelength matching a higher frequency) is 1.4x10^-2 m.

14.reason: Echoes from the two walls arrive at 0.5 s and 0.8 s; the next echo (sound reflecting off one wall then the other) arrives at 0.5 + 0.8 = 1.3 s.

15.reason: A pulse is a short-duration, non-repeating disturbance that travels through the medium -> 'all of these'.

16.reason: Infrasonic sound (<20 Hz) is produced by large animals such as rhinoceros.

17.reason: A long, soft and flexible spring (slinky) lets a pulse travel slowly and be timed/observed clearly.

18.reason: A stethoscope works on multiple reflections of sound through its tube to the ear.

19.reason: Sound travels fastest in solids; steel is the fastest medium listed.

20.reason: Echocardiography uses ultrasound waves to image the heart.

21.reason: Wave motion transfers energy (and momentum) without bulk transport of matter; 'energy' is the standard textbook answer.

25.reason: Infrasonic (<20 Hz) < audible (20 Hz-20 kHz) < ultrasonic (>20 kHz): f_i < f_a < f_u.

26.reason: Removing air leaves no medium, so sound intensity falls; speed of sound is not defined in vacuum but the bell-jar observation is the falling intensity -> 'intensity falls'. REVIEW: option D bundles 'intensity and speed fall' which is also defensible.

27.reason: Angle between incident and reflected ray = i + r = 2i = 130 deg, so i = 65 deg.

28.reason: REVIEW: Taking 'reversal after 0.1 s' as one full period T = 0.1 s, lambda = vT = 3000 x 0.1 = 300 m (option D). If a reversal meant half a period the answer (600 m) is not an option, so D is the intended choice.

29.reason: A pulse/wave transports energy along the slinky, not matter.

30.reason: A transverse pulse on a slinky is made by jerking it perpendicular to its length.

31.reason: Pulse speed depends on tension and mass per unit length (material/dimensions) and temperature, but not on the total length of the slinky.

32.reason: Megaphone, stethoscope, hearing aids and soundboards all work on reflection of sound.

33.reason: Ultrasonic waves (higher frequency) have greater penetrating power, so f_1 > f_2.

34.reason: Space is a vacuum; sound needs a medium, so a supernova's sound is not heard on Earth -> absence of medium.

35.reason: Law of reflection: angle of reflection equals angle of incidence.

36.reason: Sound in air propagates as a longitudinal wave.

37.reason: Striking harder increases amplitude (loudness) but not frequency, so pitch is unchanged.

38.reason: A long thick string makes the pulse travel slowly enough that the transit time can be measured accurately.

39.reason: Sonic booms arise from supersonic speed combined with pressure variation (shock waves).

40.reason: Speed of sound depends on temperature, not on the gunshot's frequency or loudness; so (i) frequency and (iii) loudness do not affect the result.

41.reason: Reflection of sound obeys angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

43.reason: SI unit of frequency is the hertz (Hz).

44.reason: In a compression the particles are crowded together, so density increases.

45.reason: Absorbent materials reduce reverberation time, improving acoustics; 'reverberation time has to be reduced/controlled'. REVIEW: printed option (b) says 'increased' which is wrong; (a) about lesser velocity is the only non-contradictory listed reason, but the intended acoustic purpose is reducing reverberation.

46.reason: Loudness depends on amplitude; making sound louder increases its amplitude.

47.reason: Sound needs a material medium and cannot propagate in vacuum.

48.reason: Before the main shock, earthquakes emit low-frequency infrasound (<20 Hz).

49.reason: Tuning tension/plucking adjusts the string's frequency to match the other instruments.

50.reason: Frequency is set by the source and stays the same across media; only speed and wavelength change.

51.reason: Ultrasonic waves have frequency greater than 20,000 Hz.

53.reason: Sound travels by a disturbance (vibration) moving through the medium; particles only oscillate, they do not travel along with the wave.

54.reason: REVIEW: Physically v_water > v_air, but options A and C are both printed as 'v_a > v_w' (an OCR/print duplication) and none cleanly states v_w > v_a; no correct option as printed. Best-guess A as the intended speed-comparison slot.

55.reason: Angle between incident and reflected ray = 2r = 110 deg, so angle of reflection r = 55 deg.

56.reason: Ultrasonics have frequencies more than 20,000 Hz.

57.reason: Human audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

58.reason: Sound is produced by mechanical vibrations - of a fork, a rubber band, etc. -> 'all of these'.

59.reason: Two devices of the same brand reproducing the same note differ in quality (timbre) of sound.

60.reason: f = 360 oscillations / 120 s = 3 Hz; lambda = v/f = 342/3 = 114 m; amplitude (from figure) 1 m -> '1 m, 114 m and 3 Hz' = option C.

63.reason: A note is a sound of a single (pure) frequency.

64.reason: Good reflection of sound needs a large, opaque (hard) reflecting surface.

66.reason: In the reflection-of-sound experiment the incident sound is sent down a tube at an angle (45 deg) to its axis so the reflected beam can be detected by a second tube.

67.reason: Fall time t1 = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(2*125/10) = 5 s; sound time t2 = 125/340 = 0.37 s; total = 5.37 approx 5.36 s.

69.reason: In a wave on a string each particle only oscillates about its mean position; it does not travel along the string.

70.reason: Sonic booms result from large pressure variations (shock waves).

72.reason: All listed are good precautions except 'ear should NOT be placed close to the pipe' - you must keep the ear at the pipe to hear; so that precaution should not be followed.

73.reason: Statement 1 is true (echo needs a hard, polished surface). Statement 2 is false - soft, loose surfaces absorb rather than totally reflect sound. So Statement 1 true, Statement 2 false.

74.reason: Same pitch (frequency) and loudness (amplitude) means the remaining distinguishing feature is quality (timbre).

75.reason: For an echo the reflected sound must take at least 0.1 s: 2d = v*t = 300*0.1 = 30 m, so minimum distance d = 15 m (room size).
